query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases? Earlier studies of refractory and transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys primarily examined elemental and compositional effects involving Al, Cr, Si, Ti, and V, but the reported outcomes depended on composition limits, phase readjustment, and processing. This emphasis has not resolved the oxidation behavior of compositionally complex alloys, for which synergistic elemental effects make interpretation difficult. The starting alloy was designed to retain an fcc matrix for formability and has demonstrated notable strength and fatigue performance, so any explanation should account for its integrity without compromising those constraints. Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting-state baseline, identify applicable exposure boundaries and supporting prior evidence, and state an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

This study uncovers the oxidation process in compositionally complex alloys. Our study involved subjecting an equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloy to oxidation at 400 °C under 10 mbar oxygen pressure for both ex situ and in situ observations. Ex situ observations, conducted using TEM after 120 min of oxidation, revealed a layered oxide structure. The 20 nm oxide layer on the equiatomic base alloy exhibited a composition sequence of Ni-rich (bottom layer), Cr-rich, and then Fe, Mn, and Co-rich layers (outer oxide). We chose a relatively low oxidation temperature to prevent phase transformation in the alloy, focusing solely on examining the oxidation process in the super-saturated alloy condition. BC alloys with Al, Cr, Hf, Nb, Si, and Ti-alloying elements compatible with metallic UHTM substrates with Nb and Si addition could be designed/selected to have the parameters δ, VEC, and Δχ in the as-manufactured condition and after exposure to high temperature, respectively, in the ranges 6 < δ < 10.5, 3.75 < VEC < 4.5 and 0.1 < Δχ < 0.16.

decision.trend: Research on high-entropy alloys has focused on understanding their mechanical properties, microstructure, and degradation behavior under various conditions. Recent studies have explored the effects of composition, processing, and heat treatment on the properties of these alloys. The trend suggests a growing interest in developing high-entropy alloys with improved strength, ductility, and resistance to degradation, particularly in high-temperature applications.

decision.why: To investigate the microstructural evolution and degradation mechanisms of the Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy under elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases, in-situ TEM with environmental control would provide real-time observations of the alloy's microstructure and chemical composition. This approach would help to elucidate the synergistic elemental effects and degradation mechanisms, ultimately informing the development of high-entropy alloys with improved resistance to degradation.
